title: Immunoassay Formats: Competitive vs Sandwich and the Hook Effect
summary: Explain why competitive immunoassay signal falls as analyte rises while sandwich signal rises, match each format to small or large analytes, and recognize and resolve the high-dose hook effect by dilution.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 45 Hits 1 and 3 and Traps 1 and 2 (first lesson for Ch. 45). Checked against Ghazal 2022, Agarwal 2010 and Hunsaker 2024. Nuance: the reviewer ties the hook to “one-step assays with limited antibody”; Ghazal 2022 describes it as specific to the sandwich (excess-reagent) format, reduced by excess antibody or smaller sample volume. Not taught: homogeneous vs heterogeneous sensitivity (Hit 2, Trap 3), EMIT, FPIA, RIA history — not in the sources read.

objectives: Explain signal–concentration direction in competitive and sandwich immunoassays.
Match assay format to analyte size.
Recognize and resolve the high-dose hook effect.

scenes.title: More signal — more hormone?
scenes.altText: Two invented immunoassay printouts. Cortisol (competitive format): sample A signal 80,000 counts, sample B 20,000 counts. Prolactin (sandwich format): a man with a 4-cm pituitary mass, prolactin reported only 85 ng/mL. Question token: “Which cortisol is higher — and is that prolactin real?”

cues.text: Two cortisol samples run on a competitive immunoassay: sample A gives 80,000 signal counts, sample B only 20,000.
Meanwhile, a man with a 4-centimetre pituitary tumour has a prolactin of only 85 on a sandwich immunoassay.
Which cortisol is higher? And can that prolactin be trusted?

scenes.title: Competitive: patient and tracer fight for antibody
scenes.altText: Competitive card (Ghazal 2022): limited antibody; the analyte in the sample competes with a labeled analyte (tracer) for antibody binding sites. After washing, bound signal is measured — signal is INVERSELY related to analyte concentration. Competitive immunoassays are mandatory for small molecules (e.g., steroids, thyroid hormones) and are susceptible to cross-reactions with precursors, metabolites or drugs. Schematic: few antibody seats; more patient analyte → fewer tracer molecules seated → less signal.

cues.text: In a competitive immunoassay, the antibody is limited. The patient’s analyte competes with a labelled copy, the tracer, for the same binding sites.
After washing, the bound tracer signal is measured. The more patient analyte, the less tracer binds, so signal is inversely related to concentration.
Competitive formats are required for small molecules, such as steroids and thyroid hormones.
Their weakness is cross-reaction with precursors, metabolites or drugs that resemble the analyte.

scenes.title: Sandwich: two antibodies, two epitopes
scenes.altText: Sandwich card (Ghazal 2022): a capture antibody on the solid phase and a labeled detection antibody bind DIFFERENT epitopes on the analyte (excess reagent, “two-site”). After washing, signal is DIRECTLY related to analyte concentration. Suited to larger molecules — polypeptide and pituitary hormones, PTH, thyroglobulin, insulin, C-peptide, AMH — with higher specificity and a lower limit of quantification; prone to endogenous antibodies, biotin, and the hook effect. Back to the cortisol: competitive format → sample B (20,000 counts) has the HIGHER cortisol.

cues.text: In a sandwich, or two-site, immunoassay, a capture antibody on the solid phase and a labelled detection antibody grab two different epitopes on the analyte.
After washing, the signal comes from the sandwich, so it rises directly with the analyte concentration.

Sandwiches suit larger molecules: pituitary and polypeptide hormones, PTH, insulin, C-peptide, thyroglobulin. They are more specific, but vulnerable to interfering antibodies, biotin and the hook effect.
Back to cortisol, a competitive assay: lower signal means more cortisol. Sample B, with 20,000 counts, has the higher level.

scenes.title: The hook effect
scenes.altText: Hook card (Ghazal 2022; Agarwal 2010): antigen–antibody complex formation depends on the relative proportions of antigen and antibody; a relative excess impairs immune-complex formation, so the sandwich signal falls — a falsely LOW result. It affects sandwich immunoassays, especially in tumours where concentrations rise enormously (e.g., macroprolactinoma). Detection: dilute the sample — with serial dilutions the calculated concentration rises until two successive dilutions agree. Manufacturers minimize it with excess antibody or smaller sample volumes. Example (Hunsaker 2024): urine myoglobin run on a serum assay risks a hook effect in severe muscle injury. Back to the prolactin: suspect hook — repeat on dilution.

cues.text: Sandwich assays have a trap. When the analyte is hugely in excess, the excess impairs formation of the antibody–analyte–antibody complex, so the signal falls. This is the high-dose hook effect, a falsely low result.
It happens in tumours that make enormous amounts of hormone, such as a large prolactinoma. A falsely low prolactin can lead to the wrong treatment.
The fix is dilution. With serial dilutions, the calculated concentration rises until two successive dilutions agree.
Manufacturers reduce the risk with excess antibody or smaller sample volumes, but it can still happen, for example with urine myoglobin run on a serum assay.
Back to our patient: a 4-centimetre mass with prolactin of only 85 should be repeated after dilution.

props.label: Excess antibody reduces, not removes, risk

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “High signal always means high analyte” (✓ only in sandwich assays; competitive signal is inverse); “A normal result rules out a hormone-secreting tumour” (✓ suspect hook effect when the result clashes with the clinical picture — dilute); “The hook effect affects competitive assays too” (✓ it is specific to the sandwich format).

cues.text: Trap one: high signal always means high analyte. Only in sandwich assays; in competitive assays, signal falls as analyte rises.
Trap two: a modest result rules out a hormone-secreting tumour. When the result clashes with a large tumour, suspect the hook effect and dilute.
Trap three: the hook effect affects competitive assays too. It is specific to the sandwich format.

scenes.title: Seesaw vs sandwich
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Competitive is a SEESAW (patient up, signal down); sandwich is a SANDWICH (more filling, more sandwich) — until there’s so much filling the bread can’t close (hook).” Tokens: Seesaw = inverse · Sandwich = direct · Too much filling = hook. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: a competitive assay is a seesaw; as patient analyte goes up, signal goes down. A sandwich assay is a sandwich; more filling, more sandwiches, until there is so much filling the bread cannot close. That is the hook.

Where it breaks: some competitive formats measure unbound label, so direction depends on design; the hook is reduced but not abolished by assay design; and other interferences, such as biotin or heterophile antibodies, can mimic either error.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Direction depends on what is measured

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Competitive: analyte vs tracer for limited antibody → signal INVERSE · small molecules (steroids) · cross-reactivity risk”, “Sandwich: two antibodies, two epitopes → signal DIRECT · larger molecules · high-dose hook → falsely low → dilute”.

cues.text: Competitive immunoassays give a signal that falls as analyte rises and suit small molecules, while sandwich assays give a signal that rises with analyte but can be falsely low in huge excess, the hook effect, revealed by dilution.

props.label: Competitive: signal INVERSE · small molecules · cross-reactivity
Sandwich: signal DIRECT · larger molecules · hook → falsely low → dilute

explanation.what: Plain language: immunoassays measure substances by letting antibodies grab them and counting a label; in one design the patient’s substance pushes the label off (less signal = more substance), in the other it holds the label on (more signal = more substance), and enormous amounts can paradoxically lower the result. Scientific terms: competitive (limited-reagent) immunoassay, tracer, sandwich (two-site, non-competitive, excess-reagent) immunoassay, capture and detection antibody, epitope, cross-reactivity, high-dose hook effect, serial dilution.
explanation.why: In competitive assays, analyte and tracer compete for limited antibody, so bound tracer falls as analyte rises. In sandwich assays, signal comes from antibody–analyte–antibody complexes; a large relative excess of analyte impairs complex formation (high-dose hook).
explanation.measure: Competitive: signal inversely correlated with analyte; mandatory for small molecules; cross-reactions with precursors, metabolites, drugs (Ghazal 2022). Sandwich: two antibodies, different epitopes; signal directly correlated; for larger molecules (pituitary hormones, PTH, insulin, C-peptide, Tg, AMH); prone to endogenous antibodies, biotin, hook effect. Hook: sandwich-specific; dilution reveals it — concentration rises until two successive dilutions agree; excess antibody or smaller sample volume reduces it (Ghazal 2022; Agarwal 2010; Hunsaker 2024).
explanation.differs: Competitive (inverse signal; small molecules) vs sandwich (direct signal; larger molecules; hook-prone).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: which format gives inverse signal, which analytes need competitive assays, and the next step when a sandwich result is unexpectedly low with a large tumour.

mnemonic.text: Competitive is a SEESAW; sandwich is a SANDWICH — until too much filling stops the bread closing (hook).
mnemonic.explanation: Competitive signal goes down as analyte goes up; sandwich signal goes up with analyte until extreme excess causes the hook.
mnemonic.limitation: Signal direction depends on what fraction a design measures; design reduces but does not abolish the hook; biotin and interfering antibodies can mimic either error.

questions.stem: In a competitive immunoassay for cortisol, sample X gives a much lower signal than sample Y. Which sample has more cortisol?

options.rationale: Correct. In competitive assays, more analyte displaces more tracer, so signal is lower.
Incorrect. Higher signal means less analyte in a competitive format.
Incorrect. Different signals reflect different concentrations.

options.text: Cannot tell without a hook-effect check
options.rationale: Incorrect. The hook effect is specific to sandwich assays.

questions.stem: A patient with a very large pituitary macroadenoma has a modestly raised prolactin on a sandwich immunoassay. What should the laboratory do?

options.text: Repeat the measurement on serial dilutions to check for a hook effect
options.rationale: Correct. Huge prolactin excess can give a falsely low sandwich result; dilution reveals it.

options.text: Report as is; the tumour is non-secreting
options.rationale: Incorrect. The result may be falsely low.

options.text: Switch to a competitive assay because sandwich assays cannot measure prolactin
options.rationale: Incorrect. Sandwich formats are standard for pituitary hormones; dilution is the fix.
Incorrect. Biotin is an interferent, not a correction.

questions.stem: Which analyte is most likely measured by a competitive immunoassay?

options.rationale: Correct. Competitive immunoassays are mandatory for small molecules such as steroids.
Incorrect. PTH is a larger polypeptide suited to sandwich assays.
Incorrect. Insulin is typically measured by sandwich immunoassay.
Incorrect. Thyroglobulin is a large protein measured by sandwich immunoassay.
